sections.rawHeading: 1 · Licensing (GOV — high confidence; strongest regime of the launch set)
sections.title: State licensing and registration
sections.confidenceNote: high confidence; strongest regime of the launch set
sections.markdown: Maryland has **the real thing: a state license with an exam and a funded backstop.** The **Maryland Home Improvement Commission (MHIC)**, in the Dept. of Labor, licenses anyone who solicits or performs home improvement under **Md. Code, Business Regulation, Title 8 (§ 8-101 et seq.)** — chimney repair/rebuild/reline for a homeowner is home improvement and needs an MHIC license. The license requires passing the **PSI MHIC exam**, meeting the Commission's **financial-solvency guidelines** (applicants who don't qualify may use an indemnitor or buy a **surety bond of $30,000 or $100,000** — labor.maryland.gov/license/mhic/mhicapply.shtml), paying the **$100 Guaranty Fund fee** ($175 at renewal), and — since June 1, 2024 — carrying **general liability insurance of at least $500,000** (labor.maryland.gov/license/mhic). *(Experience requirement and exam pass mark not re-read on a primary page in Sep 2026 — do not publish specific figures.)* Salespeople are separately licensed. Public lookup: **labor.maryland.gov/license/mhic**. Unlicensed home-improvement work is barred from recovery and is an offense.

sections.title: What the credential does not test
sections.markdown: Even Maryland's genuine exam tests **Maryland home-improvement law, contracts, trade practices, and consumer-protection rules — not flue diagnosis or masonry skill.** A licensed contractor may never have inspected a chimney. Individual certs (CSIA CCS, C-DET; NCSG CCP/CCR) remain the competence signal. The MD twist: because **hiring a *licensed* contractor is what unlocks the Guaranty Fund**, "check the license" carries more weight here than in any other launch state.

sections.rawHeading: 3 · Home sale (GOV — high on structure; confirm exact chimney line)
sections.title: Seller disclosure when a home sells
sections.confidenceNote: high on structure; confirm exact chimney line
sections.markdown: **Md. Real Property § 10-702 gives sellers a choice: DISCLOSE or DISCLAIM.** They may furnish **either** a **Residential Property Disclosure Statement** (disclosing known defects across the statutory categories — water/sewer, insulation, structural systems "including the roof, walls, floors, foundation, and any basement," plumbing/electrical/heating/AC, smoke alarms, a CO alarm where the home burns fossil fuel, and more, on an actual-knowledge basis) **or** a **Residential Property Disclaimer Statement** selling the home **"as is,"** disclosing only latent defects posing a direct health/safety threat. **Neither § 10-702 nor the current MREC form (footer "FORM: MREC/DLLR: Rev August 3, 2026" — labor.maryland.gov/forms/propertydanddform.pdf; also the form attached to COMAR 09.11.07.01 via Md. Register Vol. 53, Issue 15) has any chimney, fireplace, flue, or wood-stove line item** — a chimney defect surfaces only through the general questions: item 6 ("Other Structural Systems, including walls and floors"), item 8 (is heat supplied to all finished rooms / is the system in operating condition), item 24 (has the property ever had flooding or a fire) or the catch-all item 25 ("any other material defects"). The form also asks (item 19) whether a CO alarm is installed if the property relies on fossil-fuel combustion. *(The Aug 2026 revision replaced the Rev 07/31/2018 form; item numbers above are from the 2026 form.)* Because the disclaimer route is fully lawful, **Maryland's disclosure is functionally optional** — a seller can hand over an "as-is" disclaimer and reveal almost nothing about the chimney. No inspection is mandated at transfer; NFPA 211 Level 2 stays a NATIONAL STANDARD. *(2026 law, not chimney-related: Chapter 776 of 2026 (HB 200), approved May 26, 2026, effective Oct 1, 2026, has the Dept. of the Environment develop a flood-risk disclosure form that sellers must provide starting July 1, 2027 — mgaleg.maryland.gov/mgawebsite/Legislation/Details/hb0200?ys=2026RS.)*

sections.title: Consumer remedies and cancellation rights
sections.markdown: Two-track. **(1) The MHIC Guaranty Fund** compensates homeowners for **actual losses up to $30,000 per claimant for one contractor's acts or omissions (or the amount paid to the contractor, if less), with a $250,000 cap on total payouts per contractor unless the contractor reimburses the Fund** (Business Regulation § 8-405(e), mgaleg.maryland.gov; MHIC Guaranty Fund FAQ) from a *licensed* contractor's unworkmanlike, incomplete, or abandoned work — the strongest fund of the launch set (vs CT $25k, MA $25k under 201 CMR 14.00 — labeled comparison). **(2) The Maryland Consumer Protection Act (Md. Code, Commercial Law, Title 13)**, enforced by the AG's Consumer Protection Division, gives private actions for damages plus attorney's fees (no automatic treble — weaker multiplier than NJ/MA). Home-improvement and door-to-door sales carry a **3-business-day right to cancel** (Door-to-Door Sales Act, Commercial Law § 14-301 et seq.; MHIC contract rules). Complaints: MHIC + AG.

sections.title: Permits and building codes
sections.markdown: Statewide **Maryland Building Performance Standards (MBPS)** adopt the **2021 IBC and IRC (COMAR 09.12.50 / 09.12.51), effective May 29, 2023, with local jurisdictions required to implement and enforce by May 29, 2024** (labor.maryland.gov/labor/build/buildadmin.shtml); counties and municipalities may still amend locally. Chimney relines, rebuilds, crowns, and solid-fuel appliance installs are generally **permit work**; routine sweeps and like-for-like caps generally are not. Local adoption means real county-to-county variation.

sections.rawHeading: 6 · CO law (GOV — medium-high; code/rental-based, not pre-sale certificate)
sections.title: Carbon monoxide and smoke alarm law
sections.markdown: **Md. Code, Public Safety, Title 12, Subtitle 11 (§ 12-1101 et seq.)** applies (§ 12-1102) to **(1) a dwelling that relies on combustion of a fossil fuel for heat, ventilation, hot water, or clothes-dryer operation AND is newly constructed with a building permit issued on or after Jan 1, 2008**, and **(2) any hotel, lodging or rooming house, or rental dwelling unit**. § 12-1104: alarm in a central location outside each sleeping area; **rental dwelling units (since Apr 1, 2018) need an alarm outside each sleeping area AND on every level including the basement**; hotels/rooming houses have room-by-room rules (since Apr 1, 2017). § 12-1106 lets localities go stricter. (mgaleg.maryland.gov, Public Safety §§ 12-1102, 12-1104.) Unlike NJ/MA, MD has **no statewide mandatory pre-sale CO certificate** (some counties add their own). A permitted chimney job remains the natural moment to add alarms.

sections.title: Solid fuel and environmental rules
sections.markdown: No statewide burn-ban or stove-emission regime. Not a material content section for MD.

sections.rawHeading: 8 · Scam landscape (REF — partial; pull specifics before publish)
sections.title: Scam patterns and enforcement
sections.markdown: The MHIC's disciplinary docket and the AG's Consumer Protection Division both pursue home-improvement contractors, and the door-knock "we noticed your chimney" pitch is a textbook Door-to-Door / CPA violation. **Specific MD chimney-sweep enforcement actions: NOT YET CONFIRMED — re-run search before publish.**

story.heading: The story
story.markdown: Maryland is the **anti-Ohio**: where Ohio licenses nothing statewide, Maryland runs the strongest regime in the launch set — a genuine exam, financial-solvency screening (or a bond), mandatory liability insurance, and a **Guaranty Fund that actually pays homeowners up to $30,000** when a licensed contractor fails. The catch that makes the page: Maryland front-loads all its protection onto the *contractor* relationship and almost none onto the *sale* — because § 10-702 lets a seller hand over an "as-is" **disclaimer** and reveal nothing. So the two messages are sharp and opposite: **hire only an MHIC-licensed contractor (it's the key to the $30k fund), and never trust the seller's disclosure — get your own inspection.** And the eternal gap survives even here: the MHIC exam tests law, not whether the licensee can read your flue.
